questions: During these episodes, is the infant unable to respond normally to voice or touch?
Do the episodes start and stop abruptly?
Are the episodes highly similar to one another each time?
Do the eye deviation, mouth opening, and tongue protrusion occur together during the same episodes?
Does an episode last longer than 30 seconds?
Is the infant unusually sleepy, confused, or less responsive after an episode?
Do the episodes occur without feeding, handling, or another obvious trigger?
Do they occur while the infant is awake as well as during sleep or drowsiness?
Does the infant ever stop breathing, become blue or gray, or have a marked change in heart rate during an episode?
Is there any rhythmic jerking, stiffening, limpness, or one-sided weakness during or after an episode?
Does the infant have a fever or appear acutely ill?
Has there been recent vomiting, diarrhea, poor feeding, or dehydration?
Do the episodes occur mainly during or immediately after feeding, with arching, gagging, or apparent discomfort?
Has the infant received any medication, including anti-nausea, antihistamine, antipsychotic, or other prescription medication, shortly before these symptoms began?
Could the infant have accidentally swallowed or been exposed to any medication, recreational drug, or household chemical?
Has there been a recent fall, head injury, or other significant trauma?
Have the infant’s development, alertness, feeding, or movements changed between episodes?
Has the infant previously had seizures or similar episodes?
Is there a family history of seizures or other neurologic disorders in infancy?
Were there complications during pregnancy, delivery, or the newborn period?

results: 1. Prolonged video-electroencephalography with simultaneous recording of a typical episode
EEG: normal
2. Complete bedside pediatric neurologic examination, including assessment of responsiveness, tone, reflexes, and ocular motility
cranial nerve examination: ocular motor apraxia with compensatory head thrusts; facial dysmorphism
mental status / cognitive screen: normal
muscle tone examination: normal
limb strength (MRC) examination: normal
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
sensory examination (pinprick, vibration, proprioception): normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): limb and truncal ataxia
posture and pull test: ataxic stance and impaired postural reflexes
limb and truncal ataxia: absent
gait and tandem walking: normal
hearing and tinnitus: normal
3. Bedside ophthalmologic examination, including pupillary responses, funduscopy, and evaluation for nystagmus or abnormal gaze
fundoscopy: normal
nystagmus: direction and whether it changes with gaze: no nystagmus
smooth pursuit and saccades: ocular motor apraxia - failure to initiate voluntary horizontal saccades with compensatory head thrusts
adduction in horizontal gaze (each eye): full
abducting nystagmus of the fellow eye: absent
vertical gaze and convergence: normal
skew deviation / alternating cover test: ocular tilt reaction and alternate skew deviation in 66% of the cohort
ocular torsion and head tilt: none
subjective visual vertical: within normal limits
pupil size and light reaction: equal and reactive
ptosis / lid position: none
visual fields (perimetry): full
4. Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol, if video-EEG or neurologic examination is abnormal or the episodes persist
MRI diffusion-weighted sequences: molar tooth sign with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia; no restricted diffusion
MRI brain with DWI: MOLAR TOOTH SIGN with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and horizontally aligned superior cerebellar peduncles
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Joubert syndrome, a genetic ciliopathy caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in a Joubert-syndrome-related gene (specific gene not determined)

ALTERNATIVE: Joubert syndrome–related disorder with a COACH phenotype

ALTERNATIVE: PTF1A- or other congenital cerebellar malformation syndrome causing vermian hypoplasia and ocular motor apraxia

ALTERNATIVE: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia due to a recessive DNA-repair disorder
